clinicalPearls: Typically caused by biallelic variants in MLC1; a subset arises from variants in GLIALCAM (HEPACAM), which can produce both recessive disease and a remitting dominant form
Presents in infancy with macrocephaly that develops within the first year, often the earliest and most striking sign
Early motor and cognitive development is often near-normal, with slow deterioration of gait, ataxia, and spasticity over years
Seizures are common and may be precipitated by minor head trauma; epilepsy is a frequent feature
Cognitive decline is usually mild and late relative to the severity of the white-matter changes on imaging
MRI shows diffusely swollen, abnormal cerebral white matter with characteristic subcortical cysts, typically in the anterior temporal and frontoparietal regions
The dominant GLIALCAM-related variant may show improving imaging and a milder, sometimes reversible course
Diagnosis rests on the combination of macrocephaly, the typical MRI pattern, and confirmatory genetic testing; there is no disease-modifying therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts is a disorder of brain water and ion homeostasis. MLC1 and GlialCAM are proteins expressed at astrocytic end-feet and cell-cell contacts, where they regulate ion and water flux (including chloride channel activity via ClC-2) across the blood-brain and glial-limiting barriers. Defective function impairs the astrocytic handling of fluid, leading to chronic intramyelinic and extracellular oedema. Histologically the white matter is vacuolated, with splitting of myelin lamellae, and fluid accumulates to form the subcortical cysts and diffuse swelling characteristic of the disease.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of macrocephaly with leukoencephalopathy (Canavan disease, Alexander disease)
Benign familial macrocephaly (as a differential for the head size alone)
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to demonstrate diffusely swollen white matter with anterior temporal and frontoparietal subcortical cysts
Serial head circumference measurement documenting infantile-onset macrocephaly
Molecular genetic testing of MLC1 and GLIALCAM (HEPACAM)
Metabolic screening to exclude organic acidurias and other leukodystrophies
EEG when seizures occur to characterise the epilepsy
redFlags: Acute neurological deterioration or seizures following minor head trauma
Rapidly progressive loss of ambulation or bulbar function
Signs of raised intracranial pressure disproportionate to the known chronic swelling
reference.prognosis: The classic recessive form follows a slowly progressive course over years to decades, with preserved cognition until late and gradual loss of motor function; the dominant GLIALCAM-related form is milder and may partially remit. Life expectancy varies but many patients survive into adulthood.
pitfalls: Attributing infantile macrocephaly to benign familial causes and delaying imaging
Interpreting the extensive MRI white-matter change as indicating imminent severe cognitive collapse, which is usually late
Missing the distinct improving-imaging pattern of the dominant GLIALCAM variant
Overlooking head-trauma-precipitated seizures as a recognised feature
references: GeneReviews: Megalencephalic Leukoencephalopathy with Subcortical Cysts
van der Knaap and Valk, Magnetic Resonance of Myelination and Myelin Disorders
management: Recognise that no disease-modifying therapy exists, so care centres on supportive and symptomatic management of the leukoencephalopathy
Control the frequently associated epilepsy with antiseizure medication
Provide physiotherapy, occupational therapy and antispasticity measures for the slowly progressive gait disturbance, ataxia and spasticity
Advise avoidance of and prompt assessment after minor head trauma, which can precipitate seizures or acute deterioration
Offer educational support and monitor cognition, given the usually mild and late cognitive decline
Undertake regular neurological review with serial MRI to track white-matter swelling and cyst evolution
Provide genetic counselling for the recessive MLC1 and GLIALCAM forms and the milder remitting dominant GLIALCAM form
